claims.text: The target material is a multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy, exemplified by an AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic HEA.
The target eutectic HEA naturally develops a high-temperature passivating oxide film.
A continuous oxide film at elevated temperature provides corrosion resistance to the alloy.
Sliding wear mechanically disrupts or removes the high-temperature oxide film.
Mechanical instability and delamination of an oxide tribolayer can aggravate spalling and wear.
Removal of the oxide film exposes fresh, unoxidized metal to the corrosive environment.
Fresh metal exposed by wear corrodes more rapidly than the oxide-covered surface.
Accelerated corrosion at oxide-damaged locations produces localized pits.
Corrosion pits act as stress concentrators and further accelerate mechanical wear.
Reciprocal acceleration of corrosion and wear produces a synergistic coupled-degradation process.
At 600°C in a mildly acidic electrolyte under sliding, both wear and corrosion processes will be active.
Relative to an intact-oxide or minimal-wear baseline, wear-induced oxide removal will increase the corrosion rate.
Relative to the baseline, wear-induced oxide removal will increase wear depth.
The total coupled degradation will exceed the sum of the independently measured wear and corrosion contributions.
A comparison between natural-oxide specimens and specimens with an artificially stabilized oxide, under equal sliding and corrosive conditions, is intended to isolate the effect of oxide integrity.
Wear-only and corrosion-only tests can be used to estimate the individual degradation contributions.

Failure of stabilized-oxide specimens to show significantly lower corrosion and wear, or failure to observe a correlation between oxide disruption and degradation, would refute oxide removal as the primary driver.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when the oxide is mechanically resistant or when another degradation mechanism dominates.
